warmup.q: For a year, the merchant dashboard's revenue job has put each payment on the day the job processed it. You fix the code to use the payment's own timestamp, and replay the last 30 days from the Kafka topic into a new table. What would the old code have produced on that same replay?
options: The same per-day totals the live job had been showing
All 30 days of revenue on the day the replay ran
Totals that differ slightly, only on days with late uploads
An error, because a month-old record has no processing time
warmup.why: During a replay every record is processed today, so the old code puts the whole month on today's date and leaves every earlier day at zero. The third option is what the live job got wrong, and it's tempting because it is true of the live path: there, the processing minute is almost always the payment's minute, and only late uploads land on the wrong day. A replay breaks that coincidence for every record at once. The fourth option fails because processing time is never stored: it's whatever the clock says when the job runs.

sections.h: One payment is written once and ends up in five stores
sections.html:
At a payments company, a card payment is written to PostgreSQL once. Within a second it also exists in four other places: an OpenSearch index, so support can find it by the last four digits of the card; a Redis cache that holds each merchant's balance for the dashboard; a fraud-feature store that keeps each card's spend over the last hour; and, by the next morning, an Iceberg table that finance queries. Nobody planned five stores. Each one arrived with a request that the others answered badly.

One database can't do all of it well, because each store is built for one way of reading. PostgreSQL's own text search (the Storage engines track's lesson on text indexes) is enough for simple cases, but support's fuzzy search across card digits, names and emails, ranked and filtered at once, is what a search engine is built for. A two-year finance scan on the primary would compete with checkout, as the first lesson of the course showed. The fraud check needs a per-card sum over a sliding hour, recomputed thousands of times a second. So the company keeps one system of record and many derived copies, the split from the course's first lesson, now across a whole company.

Five stores need a rule for staying in step. The Stream processing track's lesson on dual writes showed the tempting answer and why it fails: if the service writes PostgreSQL and then OpenSearch, two concurrent updates can land in opposite orders in the two stores, and a crash between the writes leaves one store without the change. Nothing ever corrects it. The fix from that lesson is to write once and let change data capture (CDC) or an outbox carry every change into a log. Every other store reads the log. If the log is the only way into OpenSearch, OpenSearch is derived from PostgreSQL, and it can only be behind or buggy, never on its own path.

Couldn't a distributed transaction write all five at once? The Transactions track's lesson on two-phase commit answered that: few of these products speak XA, and an all-or-nothing write stops when any one participant stops. The Try it puts a number on it. With the search index down for three minutes, the all-or-nothing design rejects 9,000 of 30,000 payments. With the log, every payment is accepted, the search index falls 9,000 records behind and catches up 5 seconds after it returns. Asynchrony keeps a fault inside the store that has it. The price is that a reader can see one store ahead of another, which lesson 2 deals with.

Both kinds of job from Part IV fit this picture. The nightly Iceberg load is a batch job over bounded input, yesterday's records. The fraud features come from a stream job over unbounded input, every record as it arrives. Either way, a derived store is a function applied to the log. The rest of this lesson is about what happens when that function has to change.

try.title: Take one store down for three minutes
steps: Run the demo from the labs folder. It plays ten minutes of payments at 50 a second, with the search index down from minute 3 to minute 6, through two designs: a log with four consumers, and one all-or-nothing write to all five systems.
Predict before you run it: how many payments does each design reject? How far behind does the search index fall in the log design?
Look at the cache, warehouse and fraud lines. Why are they unaffected in one design and part of the outage in the other?

code.title: ContainmentDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: // async: each consumer reads the log at its own pace for (store in stores) { val up = !(store == "search" && s in down) if (up) position[store] = minOf(logEnd, position.getValue(store) + drainPerSecond) } // sync: a payment counts only if all five systems take it if (s in down) failed += rate else accepted += rate

try.expect:
async (log + consumers): 30,000 payments accepted, 0 failed
  search     max lag  9,000 records
  cache      max lag      0 records
  warehouse  max lag      0 records
  fraud      max lag      0 records
  search caught up 5 s after it came back
sync (all-or-nothing):   21,000 payments accepted, 9,000 failed
  every store but search was healthy for the whole ten minutes

Three minutes at 50 a second is 9,000 payments. The log design turns them into 9,000 records of lag in one store, drained at about 2,000 a second when it returns. The all-or-nothing design turns them into 9,000 failed payments, because one participant that can't commit stops everyone. The other three stores were fine all along; in the log design their consumers never noticed.

sections.h: A single log gives every copy the same order, until it can't
sections.html:
Payment pay-77 has two events: CAPTURED at 10:00:01, then REFUNDED at 10:04:30. A consumer that applies them the other way round ends with the payment captured, forever. Every copy that applies the same changes in the same order, with code that gives the same output for the same input, ends in the same state. That is state machine replication, which the Consistency and consensus track met as total order broadcast. A log is a cheap way to get it: one position per record, and every consumer reads in position order.

A single total order has limits, and a growing company hits each of them.

  1. Throughput. One leader assigns every position, so one machine's speed caps the log. Past that you split it into partitions (the Messaging track's lesson on keys and partitions), and order exists only inside a partition. Key by payment id, and pay-77's capture and refund share a partition; two different payments have no order between them.
  2. Regions. With a leader per region (the Replication track's lesson on many leaders), a write in Frankfurt and a write in Virginia have no defined order.
  3. Services. The disputes service and the payments service each own their data and their log. Nothing orders a dispute decision against a refund.
  4. Offline clients. A phone that applies its own writes first (the Replication track's local-first lesson) sees an order the server only learns hours later.

You can't simply build a bigger single order. Total order broadcast is equivalent to consensus, and the usual consensus protocols route every decision through one leader.

So past one partition, order only what is causally related, and say so in the data. Here is a case from payments. A support agent decides a dispute for the cardholder in the disputes service. Seeing it saved, the agent issues the refund in the payments service a few seconds later. The merchant notifier reads both logs, and when a refund arrives it looks up the dispute: no dispute on record means a merchant-initiated refund, which carries a 15.00 fee. The disputes log reaches the notifier through a CDC connector that runs up to 2.5 seconds behind. In the Try it, 76 of 1,000 refunds reach the notifier before the decision that caused them, and 76 merchants pay a fee they don't owe.

The fix is to carry the cause. The refund event names the decision it came from (its id, or the disputes-log offset the agent's screen showed), and the notifier holds a refund until it has read the disputes log that far. The wrong fees drop to zero, and the 76 held refunds wait a median of 364 ms. This doesn't generalize to a library you install. Each causal link is a field someone has to add.

try.title: Two logs, and a refund that overtakes its cause
steps: Run the demo. It decides 1,000 disputes in one log; the agent issues each refund in the other log 1 to 6 seconds later. The disputes log reaches the notifier 0.1 to 2.5 seconds late, the payments log 50 to 300 ms late.
Predict: what share of refunds does the notifier see before their decision? A tenth of a percent, a few percent, or half?
Read the second run's rule in the excerpt. The notifier now waits, so what did the fix cost, and who pays it?

code.title: CausalityDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: // each consumer reads its own log in order, at its own lag val decisionSeen = seenTimes(disputes.map { it.decidedAt }, 100, 2_500) val refundSeen = ... // payments log, 50 to 300 ms val wrong = disputes.indices.count { refundSeen[it] < decisionSeen[it] } // with the link: hold a refund until its decision has been read val handled = disputes.indices.map { maxOf(refundSeen[it], decisionSeen[it]) }

try.expect:
no link between the logs:
  refunds handled before the decision that caused them: 76 of 1000
  refund fees charged by mistake: 1,140.00
refund carries the offset of its decision, notifier waits for it:
  refunds handled before their decision: 0 of 1000
  refunds held back: 76, median hold 364 ms, longest 1255 ms

About 8%: whenever the agent is quicker than the CDC connector, the effect arrives before the cause. Each log is perfectly ordered on its own; the error is in the gap between them. The fix costs latency, and only for the refunds that would have been wrong.

refs.title: Kleppmann, Beresford and Svingen, Online Event Processing (CACM, 2019)

sections.h: Lambda: compute every answer twice and merge them when you read
sections.html:
In 2011 a team had two kinds of tool and neither was enough. Hadoop MapReduce gave exact answers over all the data, hours late. Storm gave answers within seconds, but it was hard to make a stream job exactly right, and harder to fix its output after a bug. On 13 October 2011 Nathan Marz, then at Twitter, proposed using both, in a post called "How to beat the CAP theorem". The design got a name later, the lambda architecture.

His starting point was a definition: a query is a function of all the data. So keep every event, unchanged, in a master dataset. A batch layer recomputes the views from all of it every few hours, on Hadoop, and writes them to a read-only store. A speed layer handles only the events since the last batch run, with Storm writing to a database such as Cassandra. To answer a query, the application reads both and merges them: the hourly page-view counts from the batch view, plus the last few hours from the realtime view.

Two of its ideas outlived it. The input is immutable, so a bug never destroys data, and the fix for a bad view is to recompute it from the input. Errors in the speed layer are temporary, because the next batch run overwrites them.

The cost is that every piece of logic exists twice, in two systems. Take the fraud feature "card spend over the last 24 hours". The batch version is Spark SQL over the Iceberg table. The speed version is a Flink job over the topic. One subtracts refunds and the other forgets to. One converts currencies with yesterday's rate table and the other with today's. Every morning, when a batch run replaces the realtime numbers, the feature jumps for thousands of cards, and the fraud model sees a step that no customer caused.

Jay Kreps, who co-created Kafka at LinkedIn, made the case against it in July 2014. In his experience, keeping code written in two different systems perfectly in sync was very hard, and he didn't think better tools would fix it. Twitter's Summingbird compiled one codebase to both engines, which helped, but you still operated two systems and could use only the features both had. Kreps also rejected the claim that lambda gets around the CAP theorem. Every bug fix, schema change and deploy happens twice, and two clusters need someone on call. Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2nd edition) reports that lambda has fallen out of use.

try.title: Find where the two layers disagree
steps: Below are the two layers of one lambda feature, "spend per card over the last 24 hours". Read both and list every way they can give different answers for the same card at the same moment. There are at least four.

-- batch layer, Spark SQL, runs at 02:00 and 14:00 UTC
SELECT card_id, sum(amount_eur) AS spend_24h
FROM lake.payments p
JOIN lake.fx_rates r ON r.currency = p.currency AND r.day = current_date - 1
WHERE p.status IN ('CAPTURED', 'REFUNDED')
  AND p.event_time >= current_timestamp - INTERVAL 24 HOURS
GROUP BY card_id

// speed layer, a stream job: adds each payment as it arrives
fun onPayment(p: Payment) {
    if (p.status != "CAPTURED") return
    val eur = p.amount * liveRates.getValue(p.currency)
    spend.merge(p.cardId, eur, Double::plus)      // expired by a 24 h timer per entry
}
Then decide: which of these differences would a kappa design, one job for both history and live data, remove?
try.expect:
1. Refunds: the batch layer sums captures and refunds together (and if refunds are stored as positive amounts, it adds them); the speed layer skips refunds. 2. Exchange rates: yesterday's rate table against live rates. 3. Time: the batch layer filters on event_time; the speed layer counts what arrived in the last 24 hours by its timer, which is processing time, so a late upload counts in one and not the other. 4. Arithmetic: the speed layer sums doubles, the batch layer probably decimals, so totals differ in the last cent. 5. The seam: at 02:00 and 14:00 the batch result replaces up to 12 hours of speed-layer numbers at once.

A kappa design removes 1, 2, 4 and 5, because there is only one piece of code and no merge. It doesn't remove 3 on its own: one job that uses processing time is consistently wrong. That's the next section.

refs.title: Nathan Marz, How to beat the CAP theorem (2011)
Jay Kreps, Questioning the Lambda Architecture (O'Reilly Radar, 2014)

sections.h: Kappa: keep the log, run a second copy of the job, switch the readers
sections.html:
Kreps's alternative fits in four steps, and he suggested, half joking, calling it the kappa architecture.

  1. Keep the input in a log for as long as you might need to reprocess it. To be able to rebuild 30 days, retain 30 days. Kafka's default retention.ms is 7 days (the Messaging track's lesson on retention), so this is a setting you change on purpose, or you keep the long tail in tiered storage or an Iceberg copy.
  2. When the logic changes, start a second instance of the job, reading from the beginning of the log and writing to a new table.
  3. When it has caught up, switch the application to the new table.
  4. Stop the old job and delete the old table.

There is one engine and one codebase. History is just the oldest part of the log, so replaying it is the batch job.

For one engine to do both jobs, Designing Data-Intensive Applications names three conditions. The engine must be able to replay old events through the same code that handles new ones, which the retained log gives you. A crash during the replay must not double-count anything, the exactly-once state from the Stream processing track's lesson on fault tolerance. And windows must use event time, the time inside the record, not processing time, the time on the job's clock (the Stream processing track's lesson on time).

The third condition is the one that bites, and the Try it shows why. Two copies of the v2 job replay 30 days of payments. One puts each payment on the day it processed it; the other on the day the payment happened. The first puts 554,322.25 on today and zero on every earlier day. The live job had used processing time for a year and looked right, because on the live path a payment is processed within a second of happening. Only late uploads landed on the wrong day, a few a day, and nobody noticed. A replay processes every record now, so the hidden mistake becomes the whole answer.

The Dataflow model (Akidau and colleagues at Google, VLDB 2015) turned this into a programming model. It treats a bounded dataset as a special case of an unbounded one, and asks four separate questions of every pipeline: what is computed, where in event time, when in processing time results are emitted, and how a later result refines an earlier one. Apache Beam (2.77.0, October 2026) is that model as an API. One pipeline runs on Flink, Spark or Google Cloud Dataflow, over a bounded or an unbounded source. Flink and Spark Structured Streaming also run both kinds of input in one engine on their own.

Replays take real time, so size them first. The Try it's v2 reads 6,000 records at 400 a minute while 5 a minute arrive, so it needs 6,000 / 395, rounded up: 16 minutes. A topic with a month of records at 50,000 a second has 130 billion of them.

try.title: Replay a month, by processing time and by event time
steps: Run the demo. It builds the lab's 30 days of history, then replays them into two copies of v2 at 400 records a minute, one bucketing by processing time, one by event time.
Before you look: on which day will the processing-time copy put the month's revenue?
Run it again with -Pargs=100 (100 records a minute). Which numbers change, and which stay exactly the same?

code.title: ReplayDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: for (i in position until stop) { // processing time: the minute the job handles the record (today, for all of them) v2Processing.merge(log[i].merchant to now / DAY, net(log[i]), Long::plus) // event time: the minute the payment happened, carried inside the record v2Event.merge(log[i].merchant to log[i].eventTime / DAY, net(log[i]), Long::plus) }

try.expect:
v2 read 6,080 records in 16 minutes (400 a minute, 5 new a minute)

net revenue, all merchants, by day:
  day   v2 by processing time   v2 by event time
    0                    0.00          19,684.20
    1                    0.00          19,139.78
    2                    0.00          19,609.06
  ...
   28                    0.00          17,678.19
   29                    0.00          19,785.49
   30              554,322.25           6,846.18

The processing-time copy puts the whole month on day 30. The event-time copy matches what a batch job over the same records computes. With -Pargs=100 the replay takes 64 minutes and reads 6,320 records (the extra minutes bring more live payments), and the event-time numbers for days 0 to 29 don't change by a cent: the answer depends on the log, not on how fast you replayed it.

refs.title: Akidau et al., The Dataflow Model (PVLDB 8(12), 2015)

video.title: Reprocessing: replay into v2 while v1 serves, then switch

sections.h: Reprocessing changes a derived table's shape with a way back at every step
sections.html:
The Encoding track's lesson on schema evolution gave you compatibility rules: add an optional field, and old and new readers keep working. Those rules cover additive changes. The dashboard's change isn't one. v1 stores gross captures per merchant per day, by processing time. v2 needs refunds, which v1 threw away, and event-time days, which v1 got wrong for every late upload. No ALTER TABLE turns one into the other, because the facts v2 needs aren't in v1. They are in the log, so v2 is derived from the log again, next to v1.

The stepper walks through it. v2 replays from offset 0 while v1 keeps serving. While v2 lags, nobody is moved to it, because a half-built table is missing the recent days. When its lag reaches zero, move a stable share of readers: merchants whose hash bucket is below 5, then 25, then 100. A stable share means a merchant is always on the same side, so their dashboard doesn't flip between versions on every refresh. For the merchants on v2, compare the two tables. They should differ by the refunds and the late uploads and by nothing else; any other difference is a bug in v2.

Each step can be undone, because v1 never stopped. Rollback is one assignment that points every reader back at v1, and v1's table is as current as v2's. Only the last step is one-way: stop v1 and drop its table, once everyone has been on v2 for long enough to trust it. After that, going back means another replay.

The recipe has costs, and you should plan for each. While both versions run, you pay for two jobs and two tables. The log must hold everything the new version needs, so retention is a decision made long before the migration. And a replayed job must not repeat its side effects. If v1 also emailed merchants when they crossed a threshold, v2's replay would send a month of emails again. Keep side effects out of derivation jobs, or give each one an idempotency key, which lesson 3 of this track carries end to end.

The same recipe already runs inside your database. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY builds an index from a snapshot of the table, catches up on the writes made meanwhile, and then keeps it current. Lesson 2 starts there.

stepper.title: Replay into v2, shift readers, retire v1
stepper.intro: The lab's world: 30 days of history (6,000 payments), 5 new payments a minute, and a v2 job that reads 400 records a minute.

frames.say: Today at 09:00. The dashboard reads daily_gross, which v1 has kept current for 30 days. v1 counts gross captures by the minute it processed each payment. Finance wants net revenue (refunds subtracted) by the day each payment happened, and v1's history can't be patched into that: it never stored the refunds.

frames.say: Step 2 of the recipe: start a second job with the new code, reading from offset 0, writing a new table. In Kafka terms it's a new consumer group with auto.offset.reset=earliest. v1 is untouched and keeps polling, so its readers notice nothing.

frames.say: v2 gains 395 records a minute (400 read, 5 new). Halfway through, its table holds days 0 to about 15 and nothing after. A reader moved now would see the last two weeks as zero, so shift refuses while the lag is above 0.

frames.say: 6,000 / 395 is 15.2, so on the 16th minute v2 reads the last record. From here it keeps up like v1 does: a few records a minute. Both tables now follow the same log, each with its own code.

frames.say: Shift a stable share: merchants whose hash bucket is below 25 read v2. A merchant always lands in the same bucket, so nobody flips between versions on each refresh. Compare v1 and v2 for those merchants: they should differ by the refunds and the late uploads, and by nothing else.

frames.say: Suppose a merchant reports a wrong number on v2. Rollback is one assignment: everyone reads v1 again. It works only because v1 never stopped polling; its table is as current as v2's. Fix v2's code, replay again from offset 0, and shift again.

frames.say: Step 4: at 100%, after a quiet period, stop v1 and drop daily_gross. Only now is the migration one-way: going back would mean replaying v1's code from offset 0, which needs the log to still hold 30 days.

try.title: Argue for the gradual cutover
steps: A colleague proposes a shortcut: stop v1, reset its consumer group to offset 0, deploy the v2 code into the same job and the same daily_gross table, and let it rebuild in place. "Same result, half the work."
Write down three things that go wrong for dashboard readers, or for you, with the shortcut, and which step of the recipe prevents each.
try.expect:
1. For the 16 minutes of the rebuild, every merchant reads a half-built table: recent days show zero or partial totals. The recipe keeps readers on v1 until v2's lag is 0.
  2. If v2 has a bug, there is no correct table to go back to; v1's table was overwritten. The recipe keeps v1 running and current, so rollback is one switch.
  3. Every merchant sees the new numbers at the same moment, so a bug reaches all of them at once, and support can't tell a v2 bug from a real change. The stable 5%, 25%, 100% shift limits who sees a bug and lets you compare v1 and v2 for the same merchant. Also acceptable: the rebuilt table mixes old rows written by v1 and new rows written by v2 if it isn't cleared first; and any side effects in the job run again during the rebuild.

refs.title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 13 (reprocessing for evolution)

analogy: Replacing a bridge without closing the road. Engineers build the new bridge beside the old one while traffic keeps crossing the old. When the new one passes its load tests, they move one lane across, then another, and the old bridge stays standing until they're sure; if a crack appears, the traffic goes back. The analogy breaks where reprocessing is easier: a derived table can be rebuilt from the log any number of times, in minutes, for the cost of compute, while nobody can rebuild a bridge from a record of every car that ever crossed it.
world: In a Quarkus and Oracle payments stack, the Oracle ledger is usually the system of record, and a CDC connector (Debezium, or GoldenGate in many Oracle shops) or an outbox table carries its changes into Kafka. The OpenSearch index, the Redis balances, the fraud features and the warehouse are consumers of those topics, so each can be rebuilt with a new consumer group from the earliest offset, as long as the topic still holds the data. Check that before you need it: the default retention.ms is 7 days, and a fraud-feature change that must see 90 days of history needs either longer retention or an Iceberg copy to replay from. Name output tables with a version (fraud_features_v3), put the table a service reads behind a config flag, and keep the old job running until the new one has served real traffic. Temporal workflows that react to events are side effects, not derivations: keep them out of any job you plan to replay.
mistake: The common mistake is rebuilding a derived table in place: reset the live job's consumer group to the beginning, deploy the new code, and let it overwrite the table readers use. It feels efficient, since one job and one table is less to run. For as long as the rebuild takes, every reader sees a table that is missing recent data; if the new code is wrong there is no old table to fall back to; and if the table wasn't truncated first, it ends up mixing rows from both versions. A smaller version of the same mistake is resetting offsets on a job that also sends emails or calls an API, which repeats every side effect in the replay window. Build the new version beside the old one, from offset 0, into a new table, move readers when it has caught up, and keep the old one until you're sure.

worked.title: Migrate the dashboard from v1 to v2 with Kreps's recipe

steps.say: Size the replay. The new job must read the whole history while new records keep arriving. If it reads R records a minute, L arrive each minute and H are already in the log, it catches up after H / (R - L) minutes. If R isn't much bigger than L, it never catches up.
steps.code:
H = 6,000 records of history
R = 400 records a minute (the v2 job)
L = 5 records a minute (live traffic)

minutes = ceil(6,000 / (400 - 5)) = ceil(15.19) = 16

steps.say: Start v2 from offset 0, into its own table. A new job position starts at the beginning of the log; in Kafka terms, a new consumer group with auto.offset.reset=earliest and an output table with a new name.
steps.code: fun startV2(view: View, batch: Int): Job { check(v2 == null) { "v2 is already running" } require(view !== v1.view) { "v2 needs its own table" } return Job("v2", log, view, batch).also { v2 = it } // position 0 }

steps.say: Refuse to move readers while v2 is behind. A table that has replayed half the log is missing the recent half of the days.
steps.code: fun shift(percent: Int): Boolean { val job = v2 ?: return false if (job.lag > 0) return false // still replaying percentOnV2 = percent // one assignment: atomic return true }

steps.say: Move a stable share, and read each merchant from one table. The bucket comes from the merchant id, so the same merchant always gets the same version.
steps.code: fun read(merchant: String, day: Long): Answer { val job = if (bucketOf(merchant) < percentOnV2) v2!! else v1 return Answer(job.name, job.view.cents(merchant, day)) }

steps.say: Keep the way back until the end. Rollback works while v1 runs; retiring v1 is allowed only at 100%, and after it rollback is refused.
steps.code: fun rollback() { check(!v1Retired) { "v1 is retired; there is nothing to roll back to" } percentOnV2 = 0 } fun retireV1() { check(percentOnV2 == 100) { "move every reader to v2 first" } v1.stop() // drops daily_gross v1Retired = true }

lab.title: Replay a month into v2 and cut over without losing a reader
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder. All 10 fail.

Read Log.kt and World.kt; both are finished. EventLog is the retained log, Job is a stream job with its own position and a lag, and World plays 30 days of history through v1, then moves one minute per tick with 5 new payments. Its first live payment is a late upload from yesterday 23:50.
In Migration.kt, write startV2, shift, rollback, retireV1 and read. Each is two to four lines; the KDoc says when to refuse. The six tests in MigrationTest pass.

Now look at ReprocessingTest: its three tests still fail. DailyNet in Views.kt copied v1's bucketing by processedAt. Read the failure for replay does not pile thirty days of revenue into today, then fix the one line so each record counts on the day it happened.

Run the tests again until all 10 pass. ReplayPropertyTest uses jqwik: it replays 30 random worlds with random batch sizes and checks that v2 always equals the batch answer, however the replay was chunked.
hints: startV2: Job("v2", log, view, batch) already starts at position 0. Store it in v2 before returning it, and check(v2 == null) first.
shift: val job = v2 ?: return false, then return false while job.lag > 0. Set percentOnV2 only when you return true.
read: if (bucketOf(merchant) < percentOnV2) v2!! else v1 picks the job; Answer(job.name, job.view.cents(merchant, day)) is the answer.
DailyNet.apply: the record carries e.eventTime. dayOf(e.eventTime) is the day the payment happened; processedAt is the day this job ran.

drill.title: Kreps's recipe from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the four steps of Kreps's reprocessing recipe, the three things one engine needs to run both history and live data, and the condition for shift to accept.

answer.html:
Recipe
1. Retain the input log as long as you may need to reprocess (30 days -> retain 30 days).
2. Start a second job with the new code, from offset 0, writing a NEW table.
3. When it has caught up, switch readers to the new table.
4. Stop the old job and delete the old table (keep both briefly for rollback).

One engine for batch and stream needs
- replayable input (the retained log, or files on object storage)
- exactly-once state: a crash mid-replay doesn't double-count
- event-time windows: during a replay, processing time is "now" for every record

shift(percent) accepts only when v2 exists and v2.lag == 0;
rollback only while v1 still runs; retire v1 only at 100%.

recap: A company has one system of record per fact and many derived stores. Feed them all from one log (CDC or an outbox) so each is behind at worst, never on its own path.

A log gives every consumer the same order, which is what keeps copies identical. One total order stops at one leader's throughput, at regions, at service boundaries and at offline clients; past that, order per key and carry causal links in the data.
Lambda ran the same logic in a batch layer and a speed layer and merged them at query time. Its lasting ideas are immutable input and recomputation; its flaw is two codebases that drift.
Kappa keeps the input in a log, runs a second copy of the job from offset 0 into a new table, switches readers when it has caught up, and only then retires the old one.
One engine can do both history and live data only with replayable input, exactly-once state and event-time windows. Processing-time windows put a whole replay into today.
Reprocessing is how you change a derived table's shape: two versions side by side, a stable share of readers moved at a time, and rollback until the old version is retired.

explain.prompt: Your team lead asks why the fraud-features migration will take a week of overlap instead of a deploy on Tuesday. Explain the plan and what each part protects against.
explain.answer: The features are derived from the payments topic, so the new version is built from that topic, not from the old table. On Tuesday we start a second job with the new code, a new consumer group from the earliest offset, writing a new table, while the old job keeps serving. It needs a few hours to read 90 days, which is why we raised the topic's retention last month. Nothing moves until its lag is zero, because a half-replayed table is missing the most recent days. Then we move a stable share of cards to the new table, 5%, then 25%, then everyone, and compare old and new features for the same cards; the only differences should be the ones we meant to make. Rollback is a config switch to the old table, which stays current because the old job never stops. After a week at 100% with clean comparisons, we stop the old job and drop its table. The new job uses event time, so the replay gives the same answer the live path will, and it only writes features: anything that sends alerts reads them, rather than running inside the job.

deeper.html:
Where kappa's ideas came from. Kreps's December 2013 essay on the LinkedIn engineering blog, "The Log: What every software engineer should know about real-time data's unifying abstraction", argued that a company's data flow looks like one big database, with the log as its commit log and every derived system as an index. Kappa is that essay applied to code changes.

Lambda's original post is worth reading for what it got right. Marz's "How to beat the CAP theorem" is mostly an argument for immutable data and recomputation: complexity comes from mutable state and incremental updates, so isolate them in a layer whose errors are temporary. The batch layer was, in effect, a scheduled reprocessing job. Kappa kept that idea and removed the second codebase.

The Dataflow model's four questions (what, where, when, how) are how Beam, and in a different vocabulary Flink, describe every pipeline. "When" is answered by watermarks and triggers: a watermark is the engine's estimate that no more events before time T will arrive, and a trigger says when to emit a result, possibly early and then refined. The Stream processing track's lesson on time builds these.

Reprocessing at scale. A month of a busy topic can be billions of records, so teams often bootstrap the new job from a snapshot (a lakehouse table, or the old job's state) and then continue from the log at the offset the snapshot was taken at. That is the same snapshot-then-catch-up pattern lesson 2 finds inside CREATE INDEX.

The framing of data integration, the limits of total ordering, and the unification of batch and stream follow Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 13, which treats the topic as an opinionated philosophy of streaming systems and says so.

sources.title: Jay Kreps, Questioning the Lambda Architecture (O'Reilly Radar, 2 July 2014)
Nathan Marz, How to beat the CAP theorem (13 October 2011)
Akidau et al., The Dataflow Model (PVLDB 8(12), 2015)
